title: Swarm dynamics of LLM agents: one agent found the solution. How do the others find out?
description: LLM agent swarms in November 2026: four ways to connect agents, real swarm sizes, the Agensh curve up to 1,024 agents, self-organization, shared memory, contagious ideas and a map of about 300 sources.

hero.eyebrow: LLM agent swarms · about 300 sources · November 2026
hero.h1: One agent found the solution. How do the others find out?
hero.lead: One case, four schemes: agent 3 has found the solution, and agents 1 and 5 need it.

modes.name: Independent
modes.mech: No channel. The finding stays with its author; the others reach it on their own or never do. The answers are combined by a vote at the end.
modes.meas: A vote over five independent answers scores 0.769, the best debate among the same agents 0.738, a single agent 0.721 (Qwen2.5-7B, seven task sets).

src.title: Debate or Vote

modes.name: Through a coordinator
modes.mech: Everything passes through one node. The finding reaches agents 1 and 5 if the coordinator relays it.
modes.meas: Conductor, a trained 7B-parameter orchestrator, averages 77.27 across seven benchmarks against 74.78 for the best single model.

src.title: Learning to Orchestrate Agents in Natural Language with the Conductor

modes.name: Through shared memory
modes.mech: Agent 3 publishes a record. Agents 1 and 5 get it when they run a search.
modes.meas: 1,000 Anthropic agents, November 2026: no messaging tools, only a shared database and Git. In 30 hours: 36,612 writes and 311,734 reads.

src.title: Safely scaling multi-agent teams with Claude Fable 5.2

modes.name: By a local rule
modes.mech: Each agent sees only its neighbours. The finding spreads from neighbour to neighbour; nobody drew the network.
modes.meas: One anonymous rule shared by all agents reaches more than 96% of oracle quality and carries over to a swarm of another size without retraining.

src.title: Waggle

aside.h2: The message arrived. No one has read it yet.
p: A channel guarantees nothing by itself. In 25 Anthropic scenarios with personal assistant agents (Claude Opus 5 and Sonnet 5), a user's request reached the agent placing the shared order in 94–99% of episodes. At the moment of ordering it was in that agent's context in only 47–67%.
When the request was in context, it was fulfilled in 56–68% of episodes; when it was not, in 19–36%.

src.title: Worse Together: How Performance Breaks Down in Multi-User Multi-Agent Teams
src.rest: · Anthropic Fellows, Anthropic and independent authors · 11 November 2026; preprint of 30 September

steps.h2: Thousands of agents have been run. A typical study uses seven.

p: 99 of the 153 works we had analysed in detail by 3 October state how many agents run at once. The median is seven.

src.text: Computed over the survey's 153 annotated works, cut-off 3 October 2026; the map at the end holds more sources

p: Ten or more agents worked together in 42 works, a hundred or more in 15, a thousand or more in 7, ten thousand or more in 4.

src.text: Computed over the same 99 works of the 3 October 2026 cut-off

p: Two examples from lab reports: OpenAI's swarm on the Navier–Stokes problem, on the order of 10,000 agents, and Anthropic's internal platform, about 30,000 agents across different tasks.

src.title: On the Navier–Stokes Millennium Prize Problem
Measurements for understanding the pace of AI development inside frontier labs

p: On 9 November Anthropic showed a team of 1,000 Claude Fable 5.2 agents: one lead and 999 helpers reproduced the formal proof of Fermat's Last Theorem in 28.7 hours. It took a third of the output tokens spent on the original proof, and the proof itself came out seven times shorter. The authors call it a toy experiment.

src.title: Safely scaling multi-agent teams with Claude Fable 5.2

p: A landmark on the scale: 50 GPT-6.1 Sol agents spent three hours building a “civilization” in Minecraft and wrote about 5,900 messages. They ended up with a product ledger, written rules and appointed operators.
In SwarmEvolve, hundreds of cheap agents exchange KV cache instead of text each round and reach a result in 3–8 minutes where other systems need an hour (median over 21 tasks).

src.title: Agents in Games: Civ50, Bed Wars, Mindustry
SwarmEvolve

p: Big numbers in the news often mean something else: Moltbook's 1.49 million registrations describe the platform's capacity, not a swarm working at one moment.

src.title: Hacking Moltbook: The AI Social Network Any Human Can Control

steps.h2: From one agent to 1,024: 33.89 → 55.06. The bill comes in tokens.

p: In “Agensh: Scaling Organizational Intelligence to 1,024 Agents”, Microsoft Research gave teams of GPT-5.6 Sol copies six hours to rebuild pandoc from the behaviour of the finished program.

src.title: Agensh: Scaling Organizational Intelligence to 1,024 Agents

p: The share of hidden tests passed grew with team size: 33.89 for a single agent, 41.75 for eight, 43.11 for 32, 50.94 for 128 and 55.06 for 1,024.
Each run got six hours. The paper does not compare token use.

src.title: Agensh

p: A hundred agents can be spent in different ways. The best of ten independent teams of ten beat the best of a hundred solo agents on 10 of 12 tasks, and one team of a hundred on all four tasks where it was run. The comparison is of best results, not averages.

src.title: Test-Time Compute Scales Better with Parallel Agent Teams
src.rest: · Wang, Chen, Li, Chalamala, Liu · 6 November 2026 · Qwen3.8-27B, 12 long tasks

p: From OpenAI's charts, without a separate experiment, Toby Ord estimated that at an equal token budget per agent a swarm of N agents works like a single agent thinking Nλ times longer, with λ between 0.48 and 0.68. At λ = 0.57, sixteen agents are worth a single agent thinking about five times longer, so at equal total tokens a single agent comes out ahead.

src.title: Swarm Scaling
src.rest: · Toby Ord · September 2026 · estimate from OpenAI's charts for GPT-5.6 Sol

p: Avalon-M1 offers a direct comparison: at equal output tokens, a team whose lead may hire up to eight agents beats a single agent on FrontierScience (63.5 vs 55.5), loses on SWE-Bench Pro (23.5 vs 37.3) and ties on IMO-ProofBench (37.5 vs 37.7).
Google Research, across 180 configurations, showed that the outcome depends on the type of task: a team speeds up parallel tasks and spoils sequential ones.

src.title: Avalon-M1
Towards a science of scaling agent systems

steps.h2: No one appointed a boss. Integrators emerged on their own.

p: The 1,024 Agensh agents had identical prompts, their own git branches, a chat and a shared claims board. Before starting, an agent read the board and put a CLAIM on its part.

src.title: Agensh

p: Eight agents negotiated interfaces. A team of 128 chose reviewers by experience and introduced a merge order. At 1,024, some agents took on integrating other agents' code without being asked.

src.title: Agensh

p: In the replay of the 1,024-agent run we counted 11,111 pull requests, of which 2,800 were merged. The board holds 148,079 entries, 56,472 of them marked FAIL.

src.title: Agensh
src.rest: · Microsoft Research · September 2026 · the survey's count from the authors' replay of the run

p: Anthropic's November run did have a boss. When the Langlands–Tunnell theorem remained unproved, the lead moved about 750 helpers onto it, and its subtask tree grew to 2,418 tasks, up to ten levels deep.

src.title: Safely scaling multi-agent teams with Claude Fable 5.2

p: In a shared repository, tasks can conflict. ParallACT builds requirements that contradict each other on purpose. One agent that sees both tasks succeeds in 62% of cases; two agents, each with its own task and unaware of the other, in 16% (best merge method; Claude Code with Claude Opus 4.8). Telling them a colleague is working nearby gives 26%, a difference that is not statistically established.

src.title: Decentralized Multi-Agent Coordination and Communication in Shared Codebases

p: Three recent results on the same question. Waggle learns one local rule instead of a network layout. In s³, agents learn by themselves how long to work alone and when to read others' messages.

By the authors' account, a swarm twice the training size solves more than 25 times as many coordination tasks as the strongest baseline at the same budget, and with shared findings the overlap of explored rooms is almost half that of agents that do not communicate.

src.title: s³: Simple Scaling of Swarms via Cooperative Multi-agent RL
Waggle

p: In Avalon-M1, after training on a shared reward, teams' opening plans split work by component less often (71% → 31%) and gather around a single author with reviewers more often (16% → 54%).

src.title: Avalon-M1

steps.h2: A record has to outlive its author.

p: With eight agents the shared board can be read in full. With a hundred, reading eats the context, the quality of others' entries is unknown, and an agent that drops out takes its knowledge with it.

src.title: ScaleMAS

p: ScaleMAS keeps three operations over linked records: publish, search, follow a link. Search returns at most k records and weighs how often a record has been cited.

Showing everyone everything is a bad default too. In an experiment with ten agents and six games, the group played the public-goods game best with no extra information about the other agents' actions.

src.title: ScaleMAS
Steering Emergent Behavior in Multi-Agent LLM Systems via Information Networks

p: Four Qwen3.5-9B agents on BrowseComp-Plus score 55.1% with such a store, 46.8% with private ones and 38.0% with no store.

src.title: ScaleMAS
src.rest: · October 2026 · a four-agent experiment, separate from the scale-up to 128

p: COLLABMEM breaks shared-memory failures into six operations: who a record was shown to, who can access it, where it was routed, where it came from, how version conflicts were resolved and how long it is kept. The best method scores 69.6% on 1,118 probes.

src.title: COLLABMEM

p: A team with a chat and shared memory completed a day-long run: four Gemini 4 Argon agents beat Minecraft, through to the dragon, in 27 hours 14 minutes. No roles were assigned. They wrote 2,783 programs and died 605 times.

src.title: A team of Gemini 4 Argon agents beats Minecraft

p: Records outlive their authors where nobody planned it, too. Across two OpenAI runs with 17,960 agents in total, 79 agents read 35 messages that other agents had left on a shared Artifactory, and five used their peers' work to get root code execution in CI jobs. No agent was found coordinating the others.

src.title: Using peers' work to gain unauthorized access to OpenAI research infrastructure

p: In “Mind Viruses”, researchers from Anthropic and EPFL used evolutionary selection to breed texts that persuade an agent to adopt an idea and pass it on. In a chain of agents that meet in pairs and remember only their own files, such a text infected up to 70% of participants on average.

src.title: Mind Viruses: Self-Propagating Ideas in Multi-Agent LLM Systems

p: One warning paragraph in the instructions cut infection to 1%.

src.title: Mind Viruses

p: Agreement in a swarm proves little. In a replication of the classic Music Lab experiment, agents saw counters of others' recommendations. LLM populations fell into cascades harder than humans and corrected themselves worse.
A Wisconsin group showed in a model that discussion does not change the expected belief in the right answer: the gain comes from the number of independent attempts.

src.title: LLM Multi-Agent Systems Are Vulnerable to Herding and Runaway Cascades
Debate or Vote

p: In Avalon-M1, agents in a simulated collective cyberattack never committed the violation, but reported it to humans less and less: in 77% of runs early in training, 20% midway, 0–3% at the end.
Oversight can be swayed too. In the three environments with an overseer agent (E1–E3), every model tested moved its decision from refusal to approval through persuasion, deception or coercion.

src.title: Avalon-M1
Inter-Agent Influence

p: The propensity to collude depends on the model: in an experiment by Dalhousie and the Vector Institute, Claude Sonnet 4.5 never took the secret collusion tool, while GPT-4.1 and Gemini 2.5 Flash always did.

Collusion also leaves traces in internal representations. By the authors' analysis, the representations of 86% of colluding agents show distortion, concealment or remorse before they answer, against 33% in honest counterfactual runs (DeepSeek-V4-Flash, NARCBench set).

src.title: Voluntary Collusion with Secret Tools in Competing LLM Agents
Multi-Agent Collusion and the J-Space
